Most critical takeaways (data-derived)

  • Automation risk rises materially over the horizon: average AI risk increases from 0.295 (2015) to 0.508 (2035), a +0.213 absolute change.
  • Median pay grows, but is inversely related to risk overall: median salary increases from $24,247 (2015) to $36,763 (2035), +$12,516 (+51.6%). Overall Pearson correlation between salary and risk is -0.245.
  • Job resilience declines: survival rate (class ≥ 1) moves from 91.1% (2015) to 83.7% (2035), a -7.4 pp change.
  • Risk is concentrated in a few roles: the highest average-risk titles are Business Analyst (0.750), Data Analyst (0.649), and Software Engineer (0.447).
  • Labor demand shifts unevenly: total openings grow modestly from 14,024,622 (2015) to 14,838,117 (2035), +5.8%, but some titles expand while others contract.
Risk increases while job survival declines over time (2015–2035).

Geographic and seniority signals

  • Average risk by country is relatively close, ranging from 0.393 to 0.401.
  • Survival rates differ more sharply by country: highest is USA (93.8%), lowest is India (78.6%).
  • Experience levels show small risk differences (Mid: 0.399, Entry: 0.396, Senior: 0.393), but survival increases with seniority (Entry: 83.9% → Senior: 94.5%).
Risk concentrates strongly in Business Analyst and Data Analyst roles.

Salary Trends & Segmentation

How compensation evolves by country, role, and seniority — and how it relates to automation exposure.

Salary trajectory

  • Median salary increases from $24,247 (2015) to $36,763 (2035): +$12,516 (+51.6%).
  • Country median salary ranking (all years): USA is highest at $43,422; India is lowest at $12,448.
  • Experience segmentation is the strongest pay driver in the dataset: Senior median $48,318, Mid $32,996, Entry $22,924.

Salary × AI risk correlation (explicit)

  • Overall relationship is negative: Pearson correlation salary vs risk = -0.245 (rank-correlation approximation = -0.204).
  • Median salary by risk category: Medium Risk $34,710, Low Risk $34,105, High Risk $21,683.
  • Survival and pay move together: median salary for survival class 0 is $16,832 vs class 2 at $46,418.
Country medians move upward over time, with persistent level gaps.
Scatter + fitted line shows higher risk tends to align with lower salary.

Strategic Recommendations

Recommendations are explicitly anchored to findings above; adapt thresholds to your organization’s role taxonomy.

RecommendationData anchor (from this dataset)Actionable implication
Prioritize reskilling investment away from the highest-risk roles (e.g., Business Analyst, Data Analyst) into lower-risk, higher-survival technical families. Avg risk is highest for Business Analyst (0.750) and Data Analyst (0.649); these roles also show the lowest survival rates (Business Analyst 43.0%, Data Analyst 56.5%). Shift learning budgets toward pathways aligned with AI Researcher / Cybersecurity / ML / DevOps families where survival is ~100% in this dataset.
Use compensation as a risk signal, not just a cost signal when prioritizing automation mitigation and job redesign. Salary and risk are negatively correlated (Pearson -0.245); High Risk median salary ($21,683) is materially below Low/Medium risk medians (~$34,105–$34,710). High-risk/low-pay roles may be more automatable; focus on redeploying talent into adjacent higher-value work rather than only replacing headcount.
Build future-ready skill portfolios around the fastest-growing demand skills while monitoring decliners. Top demand growers (2015→2035) include Java (+5.1%) and Python (+3.7%). Refresh curricula annually; bias toward skills with upward trend and strong survival alignment in your internal role architecture.
Focus hiring where openings expand and hedge where openings contract. Largest openings expansions include Cybersecurity Analyst (+49.1%) and Product Manager (+45.4%). Largest contractions include AI Researcher (-10.6%). Align recruiting capacity and workforce plans to expanding families; for contracting families, emphasize internal mobility and upskilling.
Segment interventions by seniority (retain + redeploy senior expertise; accelerate entry-level upskilling). Survival rises with experience (Entry 83.9% vs Senior 94.5%), while risk differences by experience are relatively small. For entry talent, front-load applied AI + automation-aware skills to reduce exposure to routine-task displacement.
Data integrity note: all metrics above are computed directly from benchmark/data.csv. The dataset is synthetic (trend-based simulation), so treat absolute values as illustrative and directionality/relative comparisons as the primary planning signal.
